# Healthy ageing

> *With age, appetite fades and the plate gets smaller, yet the need for most nutrients does not fall
> with it, and the need for protein rises. The advice an older patient needs is almost never "eat less":
> it is to eat a denser plate and, above all, to eat it in company.*

::: {.callout-note}
## Learning objectives
- Explain why falling energy needs in later life call for a more nutrient-dense plate, not a smaller one.
- Explain how anabolic resistance raises protein needs, and why protein is spread across meals and paired
  with exercise.
- Describe why vitamin B12, vitamin D, calcium and fluids need specific attention in later life, and
  identify the older adults to check or refer.
- Explain why older adults eat less, and how fortifying familiar food raises intake without adding volume.
- Explain why eating alone is a nutritional red flag, and connect the older adult to a shared meal.
- Recognise unintentional weight loss and the other red flags in an older adult, avoid restrictive diets
  in the frail, and refer.
:::

## Healthy ageing at a glance: two drivers {#sec-overview}

Later life here means the older adult, roughly 65 and over, ageing in health (the stages before it are in
the *Adulthood & Working Life* and *Menopause & Midlife Health* chapters). As at every life stage, two
drivers shape nutrition, and in later life they pull in an unexpected direction:

| Driver | What changes at this stage |
|---|---|
| Internal drivers (inside the body) | Appetite and energy needs fall, but the need for protein and micronutrients per kcal rises; ageing muscle responds less to protein; B12, vitamin D and thirst all quietly decline |
| External levers (life and environment) | Who the older person eats with: widowhood, living alone and the practical struggle to shop and cook do more damage to an older diet than any single nutrient, and a shared meal is one of the strongest remedies |

The through-line is a mismatch: energy needs go down while most nutrient needs do not.
**Nutrient density**, the amount of nutrients a food supplies for its energy, therefore has to go up
(energy down, density up). The porridge builder below shows the principle on a familiar dish.

<div data-island="same-plate" data-src="/diagrams/same-plate.yml"></div>

## What changes inside: physiological changes and nutrient needs {#sec-ageing-inside}

Appetite and food intake fall with age, a change called the **anorexia of ageing**, so an older adult
eats meaningfully less than they did as a young adult [@giezenaar2016appetite]. The recommendations for
protein and most vitamins and minerals, however, do not fall in step, so the same nutrients now have to
come from less energy [@espenGeriatrics2019]. The right response is a more nutrient-dense plate, not a
smaller version of the same one; advice to "just eat less of everything" shrinks the nutrients along with
the energy.

### Protein: needs rise with age {#sec-ageing-protein}

Protein is the clearest reversal: while energy needs fall, protein needs rise. Healthy older adults need
more protein than younger ones, about 1.0–1.2 g/kg a day against the 0.8 g/kg adult reference intake
(see the *Macronutrients* chapter) [@bauer2013protage; @deutz2014espen]. The range illustrates the upward
shift; it is not a dose to titrate. The reason for the shift is **anabolic resistance**: ageing muscle
mounts a weaker anabolic (muscle-building) response to a given amount of protein, so it takes more protein
to get the same effect [@breen2011anabolic]. As in adulthood, protein works best when paired with the stimulus of
exercise, especially resistance work (see the *Adulthood & Working Life* chapter) [@deutz2014espen].

Because each meal needs a larger protein dose to stimulate muscle protein synthesis, a palm-sized portion
of protein at each meal works better than eating most of it at dinner [@mamerow2014distribution]. This spread is a rule
of thumb grounded in the anabolic-resistance mechanism, not a precise dose, because the outcome trials in
older adults are mixed.

Enough protein, with exercise, also defends against **sarcopenia**, the age-related loss of muscle
strength and mass. Sarcopenia is screened simply in the community, where a weak hand grip is a common
first clue, using cut-offs set lower for Asian builds; suspected sarcopenia is then referred, since
diagnosis and management belong to later clinical training [@cruzjentoft2019ewgsop2; @chen2020awgs2019;
@limSarcopeniaCpg2022]. Loss of muscle strength, together with the vitamin D deficiency common in older
adults (below), raises the risk of falls and fractures [@roberts2021community; @neo2016vitDsg]. Getting
protein and activity right early is therefore worthwhile.

### Micronutrients and hydration {#sec-ageing-watchlist}

Four nutrients need specific attention in later life (the underlying biology is in the
*Micronutrients, Hydration & Electrolytes* chapter).

Vitamin B12 deficiency in older adults comes mainly from malabsorption, not a lack of B12 in the diet:
in some older adults the stomach makes less acid because of **atrophic gastritis**, a long-standing inflammation that
thins the stomach lining, and without that acid B12 cannot be split from food protein to be absorbed
[@andres2005foodCobalamin]. Long-term metformin and **proton-pump inhibitors (PPIs)**, drugs that
suppress stomach acid, add to the risk, and both are widely used in Singapore's older population, in which
diabetes is common [@porter2021b12Gastritis; @metforminB12]. Testing therefore targets the at-risk
instead of screening everyone: older adults with atrophic gastritis, those on these drugs, and those with
unexplained anaemia or nerve or memory changes are checked or referred [@mouchaileh2023b12Older].

Vitamin D deficiency is common in older adults even in sunny Singapore, and what is firmly established
is the behavioural reason: older adults spend less time outdoors and cover up [@cheong2020shield]. The
classic teaching is that ageing skin also makes the vitamin less efficiently [@maclaughlin1985skinVitD],
though newer work questions how large that effect is [@borecka2024skin7dhc]. (Dosing and the bone
evidence are in the *Bone & Joint Health* chapter.)

Calcium needs rise as absorption becomes less efficient, and locally the gap between intake and need is
wide; it is best met food-first, with anything beyond food left to the *Bone & Joint Health* chapter
[@ye2023daha].

Thirst is blunted in older adults, who dehydrate before they feel thirsty; the everyday bedside signs of
dehydration are also unreliable in older people, so the response is to offer fluids proactively, without
waiting for thirst [@li2023hydrationOlder; @hooper2016drieDehydration].

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: appetite and energy needs fall with age. Why do protein needs go up?
Ageing muscle is anabolically resistant: it mounts a weaker anabolic (muscle-building) response to a given amount of
protein, so it takes more protein to get the same effect. Needs therefore rise to about 1.0–1.2 g/kg a
day, against the 0.8 g/kg adult reference. Because energy intake is falling at the same time, that protein
has to come from less food, so the plate must be denser, with protein spread across meals and paired with
exercise.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older man on long-term metformin eats meat and eggs every day. Why can he still run short of vitamin B12?
In older age, B12 deficiency is mainly a problem of absorption, not intake. In some older adults the stomach makes less acid, so B12 cannot be split from food protein, and long-term metformin adds to the risk. A
B12-rich diet may therefore not protect him, and he fits the at-risk profile to check or refer.
:::

### Why older adults eat less {#sec-ageing-eat-less}

The anorexia of ageing has several causes. The stomach empties more slowly and signals fullness sooner,
and taste and especially smell fade, which drains food of its reward [@wysokinski2015anorexia]. Three
practical, checkable problems add to these changes:

- Poor dentition pushes people towards soft, carbohydrate-heavy food and away from meat, fruit and
  vegetables; a quick check is whether the patient can chew a piece of meat [@chan2023oralHealth].
- **Dysphagia**, difficulty swallowing, is common, and although **texture-modified food** (food whose
  texture is altered, for example minced or puréed) and thickened fluids make swallowing safer, they tend
  to lower intake, so they need enriching; coughing on food or drink, a wet voice and recurrent chest
  infections are red flags to refer [@wu2020tmd; @espenGeriatricsPractical2022].
- **Polypharmacy**, taking five or more medicines, contributes to poor appetite, nausea and altered taste
  [@morleySilver1995meals], so it is a prompt to flag the medicine list for review [@kok2022polypharmacy].

Loss of appetite often appears before weight is lost, so it is an early sign worth asking about
[@desoutobarreto2022icfsr]. The *MEALS ON WHEELS* mnemonic is a memory aid for the reversible causes of
weight loss in older people [@morleySilver1995meals].

::: {.callout-tip}
## 🍜 Food fortification: enriching familiar dishes
For a frail older adult who eats little, the first move is to make the food they already eat more
nourishing; supplement drinks come later. Stir an egg, minced fish, silken tofu, ikan bilis or milk
powder into the morning porridge or *mee sua*; enrich soups; choose the *yong tau foo* pieces that are
tofu and fish instead of the deep-fried ones; put a palm-sized protein at every meal. This food-first
fortification reliably raises energy and protein without adding volume, which suits a small appetite that
limits how much goes on the plate [@geny2023fortification; @mills2018fortified]. Because smell and taste
have faded, amplify flavour with herbs, spice and umami instead of stripping it away; this is one reason
not to put a thin, frail older adult on a bland "healthy" low-salt diet [@schiffman1993flavor].
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does fortifying familiar food suit a frail older adult better than serving bigger portions?
A small appetite limits how much goes on the plate: the stomach empties more slowly and signals fullness
sooner, and faded taste and smell drain food of its reward. Stirring egg, fish, tofu or milk powder into
porridge or soup raises energy and protein without adding volume. Keeping the flavour strong works with
the faded senses, where a bland diet would work against them.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: an older man has been moved to texture-modified meals so that he swallows more safely. What follows for his intake?
Texture-modified food and thickened fluids make swallowing safer but tend to lower intake, so his meals
need enriching to keep energy and protein up. Safety and intake pull in opposite directions here, so the
plate has to be made denser instead of larger, within the texture he has been prescribed. Coughing on
food or drink, a wet voice or recurrent chest infections are red flags to refer.
:::

## What changes outside: eating alone and isolation {#sec-ageing-social}

For older adults, company at meals often does more for nutrition than any single nutrient. People eat more, and a
wider variety of foods, in the company of familiar others than alone [@ruddock2019facilitation]. Eating
alone is therefore a practical red flag. Solo eaters have poorer, less varied diets, and more frequent
solitary eating tracks with lower fruit, vegetable and protein intake and with more low mood
[@bjornwall2024eatingAlone; @kwon2023eatingAlone]. **Social isolation** in particular, the objective lack
of contact with other people, predicts inadequate micronutrient intake [@steptoe2024isolation].

Three practical points follow:

- Widowhood is a distinct high-risk period for weight loss and lost interest in food, worth checking
  proactively [@shahar2001widowhood].
- **Food insecurity**, not having reliable access to enough food, depends in older age on physical access
  as much as on money: whether the person can get to the shops, carry the groceries and stand to cook
  [@tucher2021foodInsecurity].
- Communal meal programmes work: they raise intake and reach the isolated people who need them
  [@middleton2022sharedMeal; @cpstf2021meals].

When you take a diet history from an older adult, "Who do you eat with?" is one of the highest-yield
questions.

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: why does "Who do you eat with?" belong in an older adult's diet history?
People eat more, and more varied food, with familiar others than alone, so eating alone is a red flag for
a poorer diet. Solitary eating tracks with lower fruit, vegetable and protein intake, and social isolation
predicts inadequate micronutrient intake. The answer also points to a remedy, because communal meal
programmes raise intake in the isolated people who need them.
:::

## Recognising trouble, and when to refer {#sec-ageing-refer}

::: {.spectrum}
[From ageing in health to undernutrition]{.tree-title}

- Appetite and energy needs fall: met with a denser plate
- Unintentional weight loss of about 5% or more over 6–12 months: evaluate and refer
- Managing undernutrition: formal screening and the multidisciplinary team (the *Undernutrition &
  Malnutrition* chapter)

[Ageing in health]{.spectrum-end} [Clinical problem]{.spectrum-end}
:::

The clearest signal that ageing in health has become a clinical problem is unintentional weight loss of
about 5% or more over 6–12 months, corroborated by looser clothes or a relative's account; it must not
be dismissed as "just getting old", and it warrants evaluation and referral [@gaddey2021weightLoss].
Unintentional weight loss is also the first listed feature of **frailty**, a clinical picture in older
age defined by three or more of five features: weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking and low
physical activity [@fried2001frailty]. At this
point the older adult has crossed into undernutrition, and the formal screening tools, the
multidisciplinary team, oral supplement drinks and tube feeding are covered in the
*Undernutrition & Malnutrition* chapter. The task here is to recognise and refer.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Do no harm: restrictive diets in a frail older adult
The reflex to prescribe a low-fat, low-salt, low-sugar or weight-loss diet, sensible for a younger adult,
is actively harmful in a frail, underweight older person: it strips intake and flavour and can tip them
into malnutrition. Dietary restriction should generally be avoided in older age; weight-loss diets are
reserved for the older adult with obesity and weight-related problems, and are always paired with
exercise [@espenGeriatrics2019]. In a thin older adult who is losing weight, the rule is to **raise
nutrient density and lift restriction** ("density up, restriction off"): support intake, and refer.
:::

Each of the following is a prompt to recognise and refer:

| Trigger | What to look for |
|---|---|
| Unintentional weight loss | About 5% or more over 6–12 months, or looser clothes |
| Suspected sarcopenia | A weak grip, difficulty rising from a chair |
| At-risk B12 profile | Atrophic gastritis, long-term metformin or a PPI, unexplained anaemia, or nerve or memory changes |
| Red flags for dysphagia | Coughing on food or fluids, a wet voice, recurrent chest infections |
| Eating alone, newly widowed or isolated | An older adult eating alone, recently bereaved, or without regular contact |
| A restrictive diet in a frail older adult | A low-fat, low-salt, low-sugar or weight-loss diet in a thin, frail older adult |

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Check yourself: a thin 80-year-old has lost weight without trying over the past year. Why does a low-fat, low-salt "healthy" diet do harm here?
Weight lost without trying is the clearest sign that ageing in health has become a clinical problem; at
about 5% or more over 6–12 months it warrants evaluation and referral. Restriction strips intake and
flavour from someone who is already eating too little, and it can tip them into malnutrition. The rule is
therefore to raise nutrient density and lift restriction: support intake, and refer.
:::

## Is old age just eating less? {#sec-close}

No, and that misreading does real harm. Eating less is the change that age brings, and almost never the
advice an older patient needs. The older adult needs four things instead:

- A more nutrient-dense plate, because energy needs fall while protein and most micronutrient needs do
  not.
- More protein than in younger adulthood, spread across meals and paired with exercise.
- Familiar food, fortified and kept flavourful, in place of a restrictive "healthy" diet.
- Company at meals, often the most effective change of all, because people eat more, and more varied
  food, with others.

The clinician's job is to anticipate these shifts and make the small food-first moves; when eating less
turns into unintentional weight loss, the task is to recognise it and refer (the disease end of this
spectrum is in the *Undernutrition & Malnutrition* chapter).

## The Singapore picture {#sec-singapore}

**Singapore is ageing fast.** The share of citizens over 65 has climbed steeply and is heading towards one
in four, which makes the care of older patients an increasingly everyday skill [@sgPopulationLongevity].

**National guidance applies the nutrient-density principle locally.** The HPB Dietary Guidelines for Older
Adults set out nutrient density over quantity, more protein, calcium-rich foods, softer textures and more
fluids [@hpbSeniors]. Local guidance puts numbers to the protein point: roughly 1.2 g/kg a day for
over-50s, about a palm-sized protein at each of three meals, carried by familiar foods (eggs, a palm of
fish, tofu, pulses) [@healthhubSeniorsProtein]. Yet local survey data suggest that about one in two older
adults fall short of their protein target [@mohNNS2022]. The practical response is to fortify familiar
food (see [Why older adults eat less](#sec-ageing-eat-less)): build protein and energy into porridge,
soup and *yong tau foo* instead of prescribing unfamiliar "diet foods".

**Micronutrient shortfalls follow a local pattern.** Vitamin D deficiency is common despite the sun:
around half of healthy older adults living in the community have low levels, driven by indoor, sun-avoidant living,
not latitude [@cheong2020shield]. Calcium falls short in about half of older adults, a large fraction well
below target [@ye2023daha]. B12 deficiency, by contrast, is uncommon in well older adults locally (about 2% had low B12 in a
community sample that excluded diabetes) [@cheong2020shield], so testing is reserved for the at-risk.

**Living with family does not guarantee a shared meal.** In Singapore's multigenerational households,
many older adults eat alone even though they live with family: in one local cohort more than nine in ten
lived with family, yet about a quarter ate alone most of the time [@ye2023daha]. Locally it is loneliness (the felt lack of company), more
than living arrangement, that tracks with frailty [@geSocialFrailtySg2022]. When a diet history reveals an
older person eating alone, the local referral points are Active Ageing Centres, for communal dining and
befriending, and the wider Age Well SG programme [@mohAgeWellSg2023].

## Practise: the widow who eats alone {#sec-case}

Mdm Lim is 78, widowed four months ago, and lives alone in an HDB flat. Her daughter, who works
full-time, has noticed that her *cheongsam* hangs loose, that she "can't be bothered to cook for one" and
that she often skips lunch. She takes long-term metformin and a stomach-acid tablet. Work through the
visit, from what her daughter has noticed to what to advise and when to refer; your choices branch the
case.

Progress is saved locally; replay to explore the other paths.
